source_text: Ξενιζέσθω δὲ μηδεὶς εἰ τὴν θανάτῳ καὶ φθορᾷ διακοπτομένην ζωὴν ὀνομάζομεν διαμονήν, λογιζόμενος ὡς οὐχ εἷς τοῦ προσρήματος ὁ λόγος, οὐχ ἓν τῆς διαμονῆς τὸ μέτρον, ὅτι μηδὲ τῶν διαμενόντων φύσις μία. Εἴπερ γὰρ κατὰ τὴν οἰκείαν φύσιν ἕκαστον τῶν διαμενόντων ἔχει τὴν διαμονήν, οὔτ᾿ ἐπὶ τῶν καθαρῶς ἀφθάρτων καὶ ἀθανάτων εὕροι τις ἂν ἰσάζουσαν τὴν διαμονήν, τῷ μηδὲ τὰς οὐσίας τῶν κρειττόνων συνεξισοῦσθαι ταῖς καθ᾿ ὑπόβασιν διαφερούσαις, οὔτ᾿ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὴν ὁμαλὴν ἐκείνην τὴν ἀμετάβλητον ἐπιζητεῖν ἄξιον, ἅτε δὴ τῶν μὲν ἐξ ἀρχῆς γενομένων ἀθανάτων καὶ διαμενόντων μόνῃ τῇ γνώμῃ τοῦ ποιήσαντος ἀτελευτήτως, τῶν δὲ ἀνθρώπων κατὰ μὲν τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπὸ γενέσεως ἐχόντων τὴν ἀμετάβλητον διαμονήν, κατὰ δὲ τὸ σῶμα προσλαμβανόντων ἐκ μεταβολῆς τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν· ὅπερ ὁ τῆς ἀναστάσεως λόγος βούλεται· πρὸς ἣν ἀποβλέποντες, τήν τε διάλυσιν τοῦ σώματος, ὡς ἑπομένην τῇ μετ᾿ ἐνδείας καὶ φθορᾶς ζωῇ, περιμένομεν, καὶ μετὰ ταύτην τὴν μετ᾿ ἀφθαρσίας ἐλπίζομεν διαμονήν, οὔτε τῇ τῶν ἀλόγων τελευτῇ συνεξισοῦντες τὴν ἡμετέραν τελευτήν, οὔτε τῇ τῶν ἀθανάτων διαμονῇ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων διαμονήν, ἵνα μὴ λάθωμεν ταύτῃ συνεξισοῦντες καὶ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων φύσιν καὶ ζωὴν οἶς μὴ προσῆκεν. Οὐ τοίνυν ἐπὶ τούτῳ δυσχεραίνειν ἄξιον, εἴ τις ἀνωμαλία θεωρεῖται περὶ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων διαμονήν, οὐδ᾿ ἐπειδὴ χωρισμὸς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ τῶν τοῦ σώματος μερῶν καὶ μορίων διάλυσις τὴν συνεχῆ διακόπτει ζωήν, διὰ τοῦτ᾿ ἀπογινώσκειν χρὴ τὴν ἀνάστασιν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐπειδὴ τὴν κατὰ συναίσθησιν ζωὴν διακόπτειν δοκοῦσιν αἱ κατὰ τὸν ὕπνον φυσικῶς ἐγγινόμεναι παρέσεις τῶν αἰσθήσεων καὶ τῶν φυσικῶν δυνάμεων, ἰσομέτροις χρόνου διαστήμασιν ὑπνούντων τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ τρόπον τινὰ πάλιν ἀναβιωσκόντων, τὴν αὐτὴν παραιτούμεθα ζωὴν λέγειν· παρ᾿ ἣν αἰτίαν, οἶμαι, τινὲς ἀδελφὸν τοῦ θανάτου τὸν ὕπνον ὀνομάζουσιν, οὐχ ὡς ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν προγόνων ἢ πατέρων φύντας γενεαλογοῦντες, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς τῶν ὁμοίων παθῶν τοῖς τε θανοῦσι καὶ τοῖς ὑπνοῦσιν ἐγγινομένων, ἕνεκά γε τῆς ἠρεμίας καὶ τοῦ μηδενὸς ἐπαισθάνεσθαι τῶν παρόντων ἢ γινομένων, μᾶλλον δὲ μηδὲ τοῦ εἶναι καὶ τῆς ἰδίας ζωῆς. Εἴπερ οὖν τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ζωὴν τοσαύτης γέμουσαν ἀνωμαλίας ἀπὸ γενέσεως μέχρι διαλύσεως, καὶ διακοπτομένην πᾶσιν οἶς προείπομεν, οὐ παραιτούμεθα τὴν αὐτὴν λέγειν ζωήν, οὐδὲ τὴν ἐπέκεινα τῆς διαλύσεως ζωήν, ἥτις ἑαυτῇ συνεισάγει τὴν ἀνάστασιν, ἀπογινώσκειν ὀφείλομεν, κἂν ἐπὶ ποσὸν διακόπτηται τῷ χωρισμῷ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος.
pass_a_gloss: Let no one be disturbed if we call life which is interrupted by death and decay a staying, thinking that the word for the addition is not one, nor the measure of the staying one, because neither is the nature of those who stay one. For if each of the ones who stay has the staying according to its own nature, one would not find the staying equal even for the completely imperishable and immortal, since not even the substances of the better ones are equally balanced with the ones differing according to hypothesis, nor is it fitting to seek the even and unchangeable staying in the case of humans, since some are from the beginning immortal and stay only by the will of the one who made them, and humans have the unchangeable staying according to the soul from birth, but according to the body they take on imperishability from a change, which is what the word of the resurrection wants; looking towards which, we await the dissolution of the body, as following the life with need and decay, and after this we hope for the staying with imperishability, not balancing our end with the end of the irrational animals, nor the staying of the immortal with the staying of humans, so that we do not overlook, balancing them in this way, the nature and life of humans with those to which they do not belong. Therefore, it is not fitting to be disturbed by this, if some irregularity is observed regarding the staying of humans, nor, because the separation of the soul from the parts and limbs of the body interrupts the continuous life, should we deny the resurrection. For not even because the natural pauses of the senses and natural powers, which occur during sleep, seem to interrupt the life according to consciousness, with equal measures of time, while humans sleep and in a way come back to life again, do we reject the same life; on account of which reason, I think, some call sleep the brother of death, not as if they were born from the same ancestors or fathers, but as if the same passions occur to those who die and those who sleep, on account of the rest and the fact that nothing is perceived of the things present or happening, or rather not even of being and one's own life. If, then, we do not reject the same life, which is full of irregularities from birth to dissolution, and interrupted by all the things we mentioned before, nor the life beyond dissolution, which introduces the resurrection by itself, we ought not to deny it, even if it is interrupted for a time by the separation of the soul from the body.

pass_b_english: Let no one be disturbed if we call a life interrupted by death and decay a "staying," since the word "staying" does not have a single meaning, nor does "staying" have a single measure, because the nature of those who stay is not uniform. If each being that stays possesses its staying according to its own nature, one would not find an equal staying even among the completely imperishable and immortal, since the substances of the superior beings are not on a par with those that differ in rank. Nor is it fitting to seek an even, unchangeable staying in the case of humans. Some beings are immortal from the beginning and stay without end solely by the will of the One who made them; humans, by contrast, possess an unchangeable staying according to the soul from birth, but according to the body they receive imperishability through a change — which is precisely what the doctrine of the resurrection aims at. Looking toward that resurrection, we await the dissolution of the body as the sequel to a life marked by need and decay, and after it we hope for a staying with imperishability — neither equating our end with the end of irrational animals, nor equating the staying of the immortals with the staying of humans, lest by conflating them we overlook the nature and life of humans, assigning them to categories to which they do not belong.

Therefore it is not fitting to be troubled by this, if some irregularity is observed in the human staying; nor, because the separation of the soul from the parts and limbs of the body interrupts the continuous life, should we deny the resurrection. For we do not reject the same life merely because the natural pauses of the senses and natural powers that occur during sleep seem to interrupt the life of consciousness, with equal intervals of time, while humans sleep and in a sense come back to life again. It is for this reason, I think, that some call sleep the brother of death — not as if they were born from the same ancestors or fathers, but because similar experiences befall both the dying and the sleeping: a rest and a perception of nothing present or happening, or rather not even of being and one's own life. If, then, we do not refuse to call the same life — a life full of irregularities from birth to dissolution and interrupted by all the things we have mentioned — nor the life beyond dissolution, which itself brings in the resurrection, we ought not to deny that life either, even if it is interrupted for a time by the separation of the soul from the body.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions regarding 'staying' (διαμονή) and the nature of human vs. immortal life. Pass A preserves the Greek syntax and nuances, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that adheres to the meaning of Pass A and the source. All clauses, including the comparison between sleep and death and the distinction between soul and body, are accounted for.
